title: What are Scoped Values (JEP 506, Java 25), and how are they a safer/faster alternative to `ThreadLocal` for virtual-thread workloads?
shortTitle: What are Scoped Values (JEP 506, Java 25), and how are they a safer/faster alternative to ThreadLocal for virtual-thread workloads?

s1_definition.profdef: A scoped value, finalized as JEP 506 in Java 25, is an immutable, implicitly passed value bound for the dynamic scope of a bounded operation, declared as `ScopedValue<T>` and set with `ScopedValue.where(KEY, value).run(...)` or `call(...)`. Inside that operation, and in any code or child task it invokes, the value is readable with `KEY.get()`, and when the operation returns the binding is automatically torn down. Compared with `ThreadLocal`, a scoped value is immutable, has a clearly bounded lifetime, is inherited efficiently by structured-concurrency child threads, and cannot leak, which makes it a safer and faster fit for workloads with millions of virtual threads.
s1_definition.analogy: Imagine National Bank of India gives a visitor a temporary badge valid only for the duration of one guided tour. Everyone the visitor meets during that tour can read the badge (the current user, the request id), but the moment the tour ends the badge is automatically collected at the door, so it can never be forgotten in a pocket and misused later. A ThreadLocal is more like handing someone a permanent locker key they are supposed to return but often forget, especially when the same staff member (a pooled thread) is reused for the next visitor and still has the old key. Scoped values make the badge strictly temporary and read-only, so it is impossible to leave it behind.
s1_definition.oneliner: A scoped value is an immutable value bound for the duration of a run or call and automatically unbound afterward, giving the context-sharing of ThreadLocal without the mutability, leak risk, and per-thread cost that hurt virtual-thread workloads.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** A scoped value, finalized as JEP 506 in Java 25, is an immutable, implicitly passed value bound for the dynamic scope of a bounded operation, declared as `ScopedValue<T>` and set with `ScopedValue.where(KEY, value).run(...)` or `call(...)`. Inside that operation, and in any code or child task it invokes, the value is readable with `KEY.get()`, and when the operation returns the binding is automatically torn down. Compared with `ThreadLocal`, a scoped value is immutable, has a clearly bounded lifetime, is inherited efficiently by structured-concurrency child threads, and cannot leak, which makes it a safer and faster fit for workloads with millions of virtual threads.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** Imagine National Bank of India gives a visitor a temporary badge valid only for the duration of one guided tour. Everyone the visitor meets during that tour can read the badge (the current user, the request id), but the moment the tour ends the badge is automatically collected at the door, so it can never be forgotten in a pocket and misused later. A ThreadLocal is more like handing someone a permanent locker key they are supposed to return but often forget, especially when the same staff member (a pooled thread) is reused for the next visitor and still has the old key. Scoped values make the badge strictly temporary and read-only, so it is impossible to leave it behind.

**One line to remember:** A scoped value is an immutable value bound for the duration of a run or call and automatically unbound afterward, giving the context-sharing of ThreadLocal without the mutability, leak risk, and per-thread cost that hurt virtual-thread workloads.

sections.s2_technical:
ThreadLocal was the traditional way to carry per-request context like the current user or a request id without threading it through every method parameter. But it has three problems that get worse with virtual threads. It is mutable, so any code can call set and change it, making the data flow hard to reason about. It has an unbounded lifetime, so on a pooled platform thread a value you forget to remove lingers and leaks, which I described as a classic memory leak. And inheritance to child threads via InheritableThreadLocal copies the whole map, which is wasteful when you create millions of virtual threads.

A scoped value fixes all three. You declare a static final `ScopedValue<User> CURRENT_USER = ScopedValue.newInstance();`. You bind it only around a bounded operation: `ScopedValue.where(CURRENT_USER, rajesh).run(() -> handleRequest());`, or use call when the operation returns a value or throws a checked exception. Inside handleRequest, and anything it calls, you read it with `CURRENT_USER.get()`. The binding exists only for the dynamic extent of that run or call, and the moment it returns the binding is removed automatically, so there is nothing to forget and nothing to leak. The value is immutable: there is no set method, so once bound it cannot be changed, which makes the data flow obvious because you can only read it.

If you need a different value for a sub-operation, you rebind in a nested scope, for example `ScopedValue.where(CURRENT_USER, priya).run(subTask)`, and the new binding applies only inside that nested scope and reverts when it ends, which is a clean, stack-like rebinding rather than mutation. Scoped values are designed to work with structured concurrency: when a StructuredTaskScope forks child tasks, they transparently and cheaply inherit the enclosing scoped-value bindings without copying a map per thread, which is exactly what you want when fanning out to millions of virtual threads. A senior nuance: scoped values are for immutable context shared implicitly down a call tree, not for mutable per-thread caches or accumulation, where you would use a different mechanism; the immutability and automatic teardown are the whole point, because they make the context tamper-proof and leak-proof, and the lightweight inheritance is what makes them fast at virtual-thread scale, unlike InheritableThreadLocal which copies state eagerly.
sections.s3_banking:
Problem 1 — National Bank of India runs each incoming transfer request on its own virtual thread and needs the current user and a request id available to every layer for auditing, without passing them through every method signature. With ThreadLocal on virtual threads created per request, forgetting to remove a value risks leaks, and any layer could overwrite it. This is exactly what scoped values solve — an immutable context bound for just the request and torn down automatically.

Problem 2 — Some requests fan out to sub-tasks that need the same user context, and occasionally a sub-task must run as a different user, like an operator acting on a customer's behalf. This is exactly what nested rebinding and structured-concurrency inheritance solve — children inherit the binding cheaply, and a nested where rebinds safely for just the sub-scope.

The demo binds a current user and request id for the duration of a transfer, reads them from a deep service layer, rebinds in a nested scope for an operator sub-task, and shows the binding is gone after the scope ends. Classes and steps: `RequestContext` (scoped values), `TransferService` (reads context), and `ScopedValueDemo`.

sections.s5_journey:
Input data: two transfer requests, one for user rajesh and one for priya, each on its own virtual thread.

Step 1 — handleRequest for rajesh generates a request id and binds CURRENT_USER to rajesh and REQUEST_ID to that id using where then run. The binding exists only for the dynamic extent of that run.

Step 2 — Inside the run, transfer is called and reads the current user and request id with get, even though they were never passed as parameters, and its nested audit call reads the same values, showing the context flows implicitly down the whole call tree.

Step 3 — A nested where rebinds CURRENT_USER to an operator value and runs a sub-transfer, so inside that nested scope get returns the operator, and the moment the nested run returns, the binding reverts to rajesh, which the following transfer confirms. This is stack-like rebinding, not mutation.

Step 4 — When handleRequest returns, all bindings are torn down automatically, and priya's request runs with its own isolated bindings. Finally, reading CURRENT_USER outside any scope throws because nothing is bound, proving there is no residual value to leak, unlike a ThreadLocal left set on a reused thread.

```
2026-10-26 16:25:01 [INFO] [req=a1b2c3d4 user=rajesh] transfer Rs.50000 SAV2001->CUR3001
2026-10-26 16:25:01 [INFO] [req=a1b2c3d4 user=rajesh] audited Rs.50000
2026-10-26 16:25:01 [INFO] [req=a1b2c3d4 user=operator-rajesh] transfer Rs.1000 SAV2001->CUR3001
2026-10-26 16:25:01 [INFO] [req=a1b2c3d4 user=rajesh] transfer Rs.500 SAV2001->CUR3001
2026-10-26 16:25:01 [INFO] [req=e5f6a7b8 user=priya] transfer Rs.50000 SAV2001->CUR3001
2026-10-26 16:25:01 [WARNING] outside any scope: CURRENT_USER unbound (no leak) → NoSuchElementException
```
sections.s5b_flow:
```text
  handleRequest("rajesh")
    │ ScopedValue.where(CURRENT_USER, "rajesh").where(REQUEST_ID, id).run(() -> { ... })
    ▼  binding ACTIVE for this dynamic scope only
  transfer()  reads CURRENT_USER.get()="rajesh" , REQUEST_ID.get()=id   (not passed as args)
    │   └─ audit() reads the SAME values (flows down the call tree)
    │
    ├─ nested: where(CURRENT_USER,"operator-rajesh").run(subTransfer)
    │     inside → get()="operator-rajesh"   (rebind, stack-like)
    │     returns → reverts to "rajesh"
    ▼
  run() returns → ALL bindings auto-torn-down (nothing to remove, no leak)

  outside any scope → CURRENT_USER.get() throws  (vs ThreadLocal: stale value lingers)

  Structured concurrency children inherit bindings CHEAPLY (no per-thread map copy).
```
sections.s5c_hld:
```
  ═══ HLD — Request Context with Scoped Values ═══

  ┌──────────────┐  request  ┌──────────────────────────┐
  │ Client       │──────────→│ Transfer API (vthread/req)│
  └──────────────┘           │ where(USER,REQ_ID).run(.) │
                             └───────────┬───────────────┘
                 context flows implicitly │ (immutable, auto-scoped)
              ┌──────────────┬────────────┴──────────┬──────────────┐
              ▼              ▼                        ▼              ▼
        TransferService  AuditService           FraudService   Notification
        CURRENT_USER.get()  REQUEST_ID.get()     (no param plumbing anywhere)
  Scope ends → bindings removed automatically → leak-proof, tamper-proof context.
```
sections.s5d_lld:
```
  ═══ LLD — ScopedValue vs ThreadLocal ═══

  ┌─ Design Patterns Used ────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │ Immutable Context (dynamic scoping): where(...).run(...)       │
  │    WHY: read-only, bounded lifetime, auto-teardown             │
  │ Nested rebinding (stack discipline): inner where overrides     │
  │    WHY: safe per-sub-scope override without mutation           │
  └────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

  ┌─ SOLID Principles Applied ────────────────────────────────────┐
  │ S: context only carries read-only request data                 │
  │ D: services depend on a ScopedValue key, not a passed param    │
  └────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

  ── ScopedValue vs ThreadLocal (as prose) ─────────────────────
  mutability : ScopedValue immutable (no set) ; ThreadLocal mutable
  lifetime   : bounded to run/call, auto-removed ; ThreadLocal until removed
  leaks      : impossible (auto teardown) ; ThreadLocal leaks on pools
  inheritance: cheap for vthread children ; InheritableThreadLocal copies map
  intent     : shared read-only context ; TL also used as mutable per-thread cache

  ── Call Chain ────────────────────────────────────────────────
  1. where(USER, "rajesh").where(REQ_ID, id).run(body)
  2.   → transfer() reads USER.get()/REQ_ID.get()
  3.   → audit() reads the same (implicit down the tree)
  4.   → nested where(USER,"operator-...").run(sub) → rebind → revert
  5.   → run() returns → bindings gone (no leak)
```
sections.s6_takeaway:
A scoped value, finalized as JEP 506 in Java 25, is an immutable value that I bind for the dynamic scope of a bounded operation and that is automatically unbound when that operation returns. I declare a static final ScopedValue, bind it with ScopedValue.where key and value then run or call, and inside that operation and anything it invokes I read it with get. It solves the same problem ThreadLocal solved, carrying per-request context like the current user or a request id without threading it through every method, but it fixes the three weaknesses that hurt ThreadLocal, especially with virtual threads.

ThreadLocal is mutable, so any code can change it and the data flow becomes hard to reason about. It has an unbounded lifetime, so on a pooled thread a value you forget to remove lingers and leaks. And inheritance to child threads copies the whole map, which is wasteful when you create millions of virtual threads. A scoped value is immutable, because there is no set method, so once bound it can only be read, which makes the flow obvious. Its lifetime is strictly the dynamic extent of the run or call, and it is torn down automatically when that returns, so there is nothing to forget and nothing to leak. And it is designed so structured-concurrency child tasks inherit the binding cheaply without copying a per-thread map.

If a sub-operation needs a different value I rebind in a nested scope with another where and run, and that new binding applies only inside the nested scope and reverts when it ends, which is clean stack-like rebinding rather than mutation. That is exactly the pattern for something like an operator acting on a customer's behalf for one sub-task.

In my banking work at National Bank of India every transfer request runs on its own virtual thread, and we bind the current user and a request id as scoped values for just the request. Every layer, the transfer service, the audit, the fraud check, reads them with get without any parameter plumbing, and when the request finishes the bindings vanish automatically, so there is no risk of a stale user leaking onto the next request the way a forgotten ThreadLocal would. The senior point I always make is that scoped values are specifically for immutable context shared implicitly down a call tree, not for mutable per-thread caches or accumulators, and that the immutability and automatic teardown are the entire point, because they make the context tamper-proof and leak-proof, while the lightweight inheritance is what keeps them fast at virtual-thread scale where InheritableThreadLocal would be too expensive.
